planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Jolly Bee spreads vigorously by trailing stems and benefits from ample room to sprawl.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Jolly Bee produces two-inch, violet-blue flowers with a small white eye and darker veining continuously from late spring through hard frost on sprawling, semi-trailing stems. Discovered as a chance seedling among Geranium wallichianum and G. himalayense hybrids by a California nursery grower in the late 1990s, it shares much of the vigor and near-sterile, nonstop bloom that made its close relative Rozanne famous. Let it scramble through neighboring perennials or spill over a wall or container edge, and shear lightly if it becomes untidy midseason. It tolerates heat and humidity well once established and needs little other care.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Russell Prichard trails and roots as it spreads, so give it open ground or a container it can cascade from.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, where it flowers most freely. Russell Prichard bears vivid magenta-pink flowers with darker veining over trailing, silvery-gray-green foliage from early summer well into autumn. Raised in England in the 1920s from a cross between Geranium endressii and G. traversii, this long-established riversleaianum hybrid forms a low, wide-spreading mat useful for tumbling over walls, edging borders, or filling gaps at the front of a sunny bed. Cut back hard in late winter to refresh the foliage, and shear lightly after the first flush to encourage continued bloom.

common_name: Mavis Simpson Cranesbill (Soft Pink Trailing Geranium)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Mavis Simpson roots along its trailing stems as it spreads and is well suited to edging or wall plantings.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade. Mavis Simpson produces a long succession of soft, clear pink flowers over trailing, gray-green, velvety foliage from early summer into fall. Like its sibling Russell Prichard, it is a Geranium endressii x G. traversii hybrid selected in England, but it stays a gentler pink rather than magenta and forms a similarly low, spreading mat. It works well cascading over low walls, filling gaps between paving, or edging a sunny border. Trim back congested growth in late winter and shear lightly after the first bloom flush to keep it tidy and encourage rebloom.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Kashmir Purple spreads by rhizomes and can be increased readily by division.

directions: Plant in moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Kashmir Purple bears rounded, rich purple-violet flowers with fine darker veining over finely cut foliage in a compact, spreading clump through late spring and early summer. It is the deeper-colored counterpart to the white-flowered Geranium clarkei 'Kashmir White,' collected from the same Himalayan species and sharing its rhizomatous, ground-covering habit. Use it as a front-of-border filler or naturalized under shrubs, where it slowly forms a dense patch. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring or fall to maintain vigor and control spread.

common_name: Lily Lovell Cranesbill (Large-Flowered Purple Mourning Widow Geranium)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in partial to full shade; Lily Lovell tolerates drier shade once established but flowers best with consistent moisture.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in partial to full shade. Lily Lovell sends up tall, wiry stems carrying nodding, reflexed flowers in a rich reddish-purple, notably larger than the species, over mounded, softly hairy foliage in late spring and early summer. Selected from the woodland species Geranium phaeum, it is taller and more substantial than many mourning widow forms, making a striking vertical accent in a shaded border or woodland edge. Cut the flowering stems to the ground after bloom to tidy the plant and often prompt a flush of fresh foliage. It self-sows modestly and is easily increased by division in spring or fall.

common_name: Philippe Vapelle Cranesbill (Violet-Blue Geranium with Veined Petals)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Philippe Vapelle forms a neat, compact mound and tolerates drier conditions better than many hardy geraniums once established.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, where its felted foliage resists rot. Philippe Vapelle bears large, violet-blue flowers etched with fine darker veining over soft, silvery-gray, rounded leaves in a tidy, compact mound through late spring and early summer. A hybrid of Geranium renardii and G. platypetalum raised in France, it combines the neat habit and textured foliage of renardii with richer flower color from its psilostemon-group parent, and holds the Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit for reliable garden performance. Its drought tolerance once established suits it well to rock gardens and gravel plantings. Remove spent flower stems to keep the mound looking fresh.

common_name: Salome Cranesbill (Smoky Purple Geranium with Dark Eye)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Salome spreads by trailing stems that root as they go, so allow room for it to ramble.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Salome bears large, smoky mauve-purple flowers with a pronounced near-black eye and dark veining over lobed foliage that often takes on maroon tints, blooming from midsummer into fall. Raised by English plantswoman Elizabeth Strangman from a cross between Geranium procurrens and G. psilostemon, it inherits the sprawling, rooting habit of procurrens along with richer flower color from its psilostemon parentage, and carries the Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit. Let it scramble through nearby shrubs or over a wall, and cut back hard in late winter to control its spread and refresh growth.

common_name: Midnight Reiter Cranesbill (Purple-Leaved Blue-Flowered Meadow Geranium)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Midnight Reiter's dark foliage colors best with good sun exposure.

directions: Plant in moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Midnight Reiter contrasts deeply purple-black, finely cut foliage with clear violet-blue, cup-shaped flowers held above the clump in late spring and early summer. Selected as a dark-leaved form of the meadow cranesbill Geranium pratense and named for San Francisco horticulturist Victor Reiter Jr., it retains much of its rich foliage color through the season, especially in sunnier spots. Its striking leaf color makes it a favorite as a foil for silver- or gold-leaved companions in a mixed border. Cut the plant back hard after flowering to tidy it and encourage a flush of fresh, dark foliage.
